objects.name: UAC Bypass via Fodhelper Registry Hijacking
objects.pattern:
title: UAC Bypass via Fodhelper Registry Hijacking
id: 9a2c5b8f-3d1e-4f5a-8c9b-1a2d3e4f5a6b
status: experimental
description: >-
    Detects creation of the ms-settings\shell\open\command key, or a write to its (Default) or
    DelegateExecute value, in a user's Classes hive. Sysmon reports a per-user write to
    HKCU\Software\Classes as HKU\<SID>\Software\Classes or HKU\<SID>_Classes, and the selection
    accepts both; machine-hive (HKLM) writes are not matched. This is the key the Fodhelper UAC
    bypass technique hijacks: the key is written by an ordinary user-level process (no
    administrator rights are needed), and fodhelper.exe, which auto-elevates, then reads it on
    launch and executes its DelegateExecute/default value at high integrity without a UAC
    prompt. A write to this key from any process other than fodhelper.exe or the Settings
    app itself is a strong indicator of this technique in use.
references:
    - https://the-hunters-ledger.com/hunting-detections/uac-test-exe-detections/
author: The Hunters Ledger
date: '2026-01-12'
modified: '2026-10-11'
tags:
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.stealth
    - attack.t1548.002
    - detection.emerging-threats
    - stp.4
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
    definition: 'Requires Sysmon Event ID 12 (RegistryEvent create or delete key) and Event ID 13 (RegistryEvent value set), with registry monitoring that covers the per-user Classes hive.'
detection:
    selection_hive:
        TargetObject|startswith: 'HKU\'
    selection_key:
        EventType:
            - 'CreateKey'
            - 'SetValue'
        TargetObject|endswith:
            - '\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command'
            - '\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command\(Default)'
            - '\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command\DelegateExecute'
            - '_Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command'
            - '_Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command\(Default)'
            - '_Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command\DelegateExecute'
    filter_legitimate:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\fodhelper.exe'
            - '\SystemSettings.exe'
    condition: selection_hive and selection_key and not filter_legitimate
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate system administration or registry cleanup tools (extremely rare)
    - Windows Settings application legitimate use
level: high

objects.name: FleetAgentFUD_WebSocket_C2_Pattern
objects.pattern:
/*
   Yara Rule Set
   Identifier: Arsenal-237-109.230.231.37-Malware-Repository
   Author: The Hunters Ledger
   Source: https://the-hunters-ledger.com/
   License: CC BY 4.0 - https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
*/

rule FleetAgentFUD_WebSocket_C2_Pattern {
   meta:
      description = "Detects FleetAgentFUD.exe WebSocket C2 implementation via protocol strings, RAT-style JSON registration fields, and the bespoke X-Agent-Secret authentication header. RFC 6455 handshake strings alone are shared by legitimate WebSocket applications — the X-Agent-Secret branch is the only high-confidence path."
      license = "CC BY 4.0 - https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/"
      author = "The Hunters Ledger"
      reference = "https://the-hunters-ledger.com/hunting-detections/fleetagentfud-exe-detections/"
      date = "2026-01-12"
      family = "FleetAgentFUD"
      malware_type = "RAT"
      campaign = "Arsenal-237-109.230.231.37-Malware-Repository"
      id = "ec392648-d132-4110-b47b-9e53d28f481d"
      hash1 = "072ce701ec0252eeddd6a0501555296bce512a7b90422addbb6d3619ae10f4ff"
   strings:
      // WebSocket handshake headers
      $ws1 = "Connection: Upgrade" ascii wide
      $ws2 = "Sec-WebSocket-Key: " ascii wide
      $ws3 = "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" ascii wide
      $ws4 = "X-Agent-Secret: " ascii wide

      // WebSocket message types
      $msg1 = "\"type\":\"register\"" ascii wide nocase
      $msg2 = "\"type\":\"heartbeat\"" ascii wide nocase
      $msg3 = "machine_id" ascii wide
      $msg4 = "hostname" ascii wide
      $msg5 = "os_version" ascii wide
      $msg6 = "agent_ver" ascii wide

      // Command types
      $cmd1 = "cmd_type" ascii wide
      $cmd2 = "command_id" ascii wide
      $cmd3 = "powershell" ascii wide
      $cmd4 = "sysinfo" ascii wide
      $cmd5 = "clipboard" ascii wide

      // .NET networking APIs
      $api1 = "System.Net.Sockets" ascii
      $api2 = "TcpClient" ascii
      $api3 = "NetworkStream" ascii

   condition:
      uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and
      filesize < 50KB and
      (
         // Moderate match: generic WebSocket headers + registration fields (broad — see Rationale)
         (3 of ($ws*) and 3 of ($msg*)) or

         // Moderate match: WebSocket + command types
         (2 of ($ws*) and 3 of ($cmd*)) or

         // Higher confidence: bespoke X-Agent-Secret header required (all of $ws*) + .NET networking
         (all of ($ws*) and any of ($api*))
      )
}

description: >-

  WindowsDefenderUpdate Run-key write are observed on the same host within a
  short window. Neither base signal alone is reliable (both are single,
  attacker-chosen literal names that a rebrand trivially evades), but the
  malware's own dual-persistence design — redundant survival so removing one
  mechanism does not eliminate the other — means a genuine infection produces
  both artifacts together, close in time, which a coincidental unrelated
  installer would not.

  - https://the-hunters-ledger.com/hunting-detections/agent-exe-detections/
author: The Hunters Ledger

  - attack.t1036.005
  - detection.emerging-threats

  type: temporal
  rules:
    - windefendersvc_startup_drop
    - windowsdefenderupdate_run_key_write
  group-by:

  timespan: 10m
falsepositives:
  - >-
